title: Similar employment rates between Roma and non-Roma conceal a wide gap in working conditions and dependable income
source: Source: 2025 Multi-Country Survey on Socio-Economic Vulnerabilities of Roma, surveyed communities in Georgia. Quotes from the micro-narratives study with Roma respondents in Georgia.

sections.title: Young Roma’s working life paths take a different course from the start

content.content: Roma and non-Roma aged 15 to 24 are equally likely to have a job. The sharper difference is among those without one: most young non-Roma in this position are still studying, while many young Roma are not in employment, education or training.

content.content: Without a course to attend or a first job to build on, the critical years in which their peers gain qualifications slip by. Returning takes more than an open place: training has to match the schooling people have and fit around care and the daily need to earn income.

sections.title: Roma women are locked out of both the labor market and the educational opportunities in early adulthood

content.content: Young Roma women are much less likely than their non-Roma peers to be studying, and more than half are neither in employment, education or training. Accounts of care responsibilities for children and younger siblings help explain why a course or job can be difficult to take up.

content.content: For Roma men, the trajectory of work life pulls the other way: young Roma men work more often than their non-Roma peers, but those aged 25 to 64 work less often. Starting work early does not lead to a stronger position in the labor market or to more secure jobs later on.

sections.title: Employment patterns unfold differently based on age and gender

content.content: The compounding education and employment gaps translate into economic insecurity for Roma households, which frequently depends on precarious, irregular work with no social security.

Informality is common among Roma workers at both younger and older age cohorts. When income depends on occasional or seasonal jobs, the uncertainty reaches everyone who relies on them. Roma are disproportionately more likely to live in a household affected by unemployment or intermittent work.

Among adults aged 25 to 64, Roma women are more likely to work than non-Roma women. Yet the near-universal informality of women’s employment makes clear how little a job alone says about their economic independence. For working conditions, street vending or trading in local markets offer flexibility to fit income-generating activities around care responsibilities, but they have little protection when adversities interrupt their income.

sections.title: Even a qualification does not secure a formal job

content.content: Schooling does make a difference to whether Roma find work. Roma with secondary education or more are employed as often as their non-Roma neighbors with the same schooling.

However, it makes far less difference to the job quality. Even with a secondary school diploma, most Roma who work have no written contract and no social contributions, far more often than their non-Roma neighbors with the same qualifications.
Some qualified young Roma describe being hired, then let go once an employer learns they are Roma, as one trained bartender recounts:

content.content: “I have vocational education and I am a bartender. Despite being skilled in my profession, I haven’t been able to find job. Bar owners initially hire me, but when they find out that I am Roma, they ask me to leave for various reasons. This really hurts me.”
content.author: Male, aged 18 to 23

sections.title: Families piece together livelihoods from the work available locally

content.content: In urban areas, many Roma rely on market and street trading. In Kakheti, families follow the vineyard and orchard harvests and travel abroad for work in winter. Households combine seasonal work and mobility with informal and irregular gigs.

Informal trading matters most where women head the household. Roma households headed by women are far more likely to rely on self-employment than households headed by non-Roma women, making the local market stall the main source of income.

content.content: “I am a young guy and I don’t have a stable income... I get paid daily, sometimes for scrap metal, sometimes for cleaning yards, sometimes for construction work. In short, the conditions are bad, and I really want to have a permanent job.”
content.author: Male, aged 18 to 23

content.content: “The main problem is that there are no permanent jobs in Dedoplistskaro, only seasonal work. That’s why I work in vineyards during the summer and go to Poland for work in the winter. It would be great if there were permanent jobs so that we wouldn’t have to go abroad.”
content.author: Female, aged 18 to 23

sections.title: Fear of losing the social assistance that supports the tight household budgets makes formal employment a less preferred option

content.content: Social assistance supports families in covering the costs that the income from informal work cannot meet. When that support is essential, uncertainty about how a registered wage would affect eligibility can discourage a move into formal work. One woman describes the risk as she understands it:

“...Despite receiving social assistance, it is very difficult for a person to pay rent. I can’t officially go out to work because if my salary is deposited, they will immediately cancel my assistance.”
content.author: Female, aged 30 to 49
